_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-03.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

places.why: "men began to call upon the name of the LORD" reads just as well as calling on the LORD by His name, so the verse does not plainly put "name" for the person. The marked words also take in the verb "call upon".

"the earth ... was corrupt" can mean the land itself was ruined by its creatures, and 6:13 "destroy both them and the earth" keeps the earth apart from its people. Earth for its people is not plain here, and the marked words are a whole clause.

Every bird, beast and fish "delivered into your hand" cannot be put in a real hand, so "hand" plainly stands for man's power over them. The figure is carried by "your hand"; "delivered" is not part of it.

The tagged Hebrew word is shown glossed "to own language its", and the BSB reads "according to their languages". Neither the BSB nor the words shown show a figure. Seeing one needs the word's history, which only a commentary would give.
"clans, languages, lands, and nations" is a plain list, and the tagged word is glossed "to languages their". No figure shows in the BSB or in the words shown.
This is the same plain list as 10:20, and the tagged word is glossed "to languages their". No figure is seen in the BSB or in the words shown.
In "one people speaking the same language" the tagged word is shown glossed "and a language". A reader of the BSB or of the words shown sees no figure.
Both Hebrew words behind "their language" and "speech" are glossed "language", so no figure is shown. The tag also covers only the first of them (H8193K), not the word behind "speech" (H8193H).

The tagged word is glossed "language" and shows no figure, and the two marks overlap. But "confused the language of the whole world" plainly puts the world for its people, since the world itself has no language (both readers named this). Kept at "the whole world", and the tag on the language word is dropped because it does not point at this figure.
"he called on the name of the LORD" reads naturally as Abram calling on the LORD by name in worship. The verse does not plainly put "name" for the person, and the marked words take in "called on".
"there Abram called on the name of the LORD" works as a literal calling out of the LORD's name, so the figure is not plain. The marked words also take in the verb.
The kings Abram defeated (14:17) were not put into his real hand, so "who has delivered your enemies into your hand" plainly uses "hand" for power. The figure is "your hand", not the whole clause.

"I have raised my hand to the LORD ... that I will not accept even a thread" may simply tell of the gesture Abram made with his oath. So it is not plain that the sign is named in place of the swearing. When in doubt the place does not go live.
"he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God" has the same literal reading as the other calling-on-the-name verses, so the figure is not plain. The marked words also take in the verb.

The figure is plain in the Hebrew shown, "let us ask <obj.> mouth her": the mouth stands for what Rebekah will say. But the tags also mark the verb "ask" (H7592) and the object marker (H0853), and tags can only be kept or dropped as a set. Dropped, the BSB words "her opinion" show no figure. The place would need rebuilding with H6310G alone on "her opinion".
"Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD" reads naturally as worship that names the LORD. "Name" is not plainly put for the person, and the marked words take in "called on".

"deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid that he may come and attack me": Esau's "hand" is plainly his power to harm. The figure is "the hand"; "deliver me" and the hanging "of" are not part of it.

Joseph had not yet reached his brothers (37:23), who were only plotting "let us kill him" (37:20). So "rescue Joseph from their hands" plainly uses "hands" for their power over him. The figure is "their hands".
As in 37:21, "so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands" plainly uses "hands" for the brothers' power. The figure is "their hands" alone, not "rescue Joseph".

Gray hair does not go down to Sheol by itself, so "you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow" plainly puts the gray hair for Jacob in his old age. The figure is "my gray hair"; "down to Sheol" is not part of it.

"he will die. Then your servants will have brought the gray hair of your servant our father down to Sheol": the gray hair plainly stands for the old father who dies. The figure is "the gray hair", not "down to Sheol".
After "their oppressors" (3:7), "rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians" plainly uses "hand" for Egypt's power. The figure is "the hand"; "rescue them" and the hanging "of" are not part of it.

The Hebrew shown, "I will be with mouth your", answers "Who gave man his mouth?" (4:11), so it may mean the real mouth Moses said was slow, not speech in its place. The tags also mark "I will be" (H1961) and "with" (H5973A), which carry nothing. Dropping them would leave the BSB "as you speak" showing no figure.

In "put the words in his mouth" the mouth is close to the literal place speech comes from, so that mark is not a plain metonymy. The tags also mark "I will be" and "with", which carry nothing. Dropping the tags would leave "help both of you to speak" showing no figure in the BSB.

The Hebrew shown, "he will become of you <into> a mouth", plainly calls Aaron Moses' mouth, the organ named for the one who speaks for him. The tag on H6310G is right, but the marked BSB word "and" carries nothing. The mark moves to "spokesman".

In "shall not eat the Passover", Passover is the ordinary name of the meal and of the lamb itself (12:46 "It must be eaten"). The verse shows no figure plainly, and the marked words also take in "eat".

In "saved Israel from the hand of the Egyptians", a whole people has no single hand, so "hand" plainly stands for Egypt's power. The figure is in "the hand". "saved Israel" and the hanging "of" are not part of it.
"the house of Israel called the bread manna": "house of Israel" is a set name for the nation, and a reader would not see a figure in it without a commentary.

In "delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh", Moses never stood under a real blade (he fled Pharaoh, who sought to kill him), so "sword" plainly stands for Pharaoh's power to put him to death. The word carrying the figure is "the sword", not "from".

In "rescued from the hand of the Egyptians", with "all the hardships" in 18:8, "hand" plainly stands for their power. The marked words wrongly took in "rescued" and a hanging "of". The figure is "the hand".
"tell the house of Jacob": this is a set name for the people, used in its ordinary sense, not a figure a reader would see.

In "I will deliver the inhabitants into your hand", the peoples of a whole land are put under Israel's power, not into a literal hand. The figure is "your hand". "deliver the inhabitants" is not part of it.

"so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things": the words do not plainly show that "iniquity" is put for its guilt or penalty. The Hebrew word itself also means guilt, so it takes a commentary to see a figure here.

The Hebrew "recorded on [the] mouth of Moses" (BSB "at Moses' command") plainly uses "mouth" for his spoken word. But the tags also mark the preposition "on" (H5921A) and the name "Moses" (H4872), which do not carry the figure, and they cannot be cut down to H6310I alone here. Stripping the tags would leave only the BSB "command", where no figure shows. Dropped for now. It could come back with only H6310I tagged and the word "command" marked.
"in the sight of all the house of Israel": a set name for the nation, not a figure that is plain in the verse.
"he shall bear the iniquity" reads plainly as "he is guilty". The verse does not show "iniquity" standing for its punishment, and the Hebrew word also means guilt. Not plain without a commentary.

"the one who eats of it shall bear his iniquity" reads as carrying his own guilt. Reading "iniquity" as named for its penalty is something a commentary supplies, not something the verse plainly shows.
"your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn": a set name for the people, not a figure a reader would see without a commentary.
"Anyone from the house of Israel": a set name for the nation used in its ordinary sense.

"anyone from the house of Israel" is the nation's stock name, and "house" for a family line is an ordinary sense of the word. A reader is not plainly shown one thing named for another, so with that doubt it stays out.
"If anyone from the house of Israel" uses the usual name for the nation. The family sense of "house" is ordinary, so the figure is not plainly seen and the place stays out.

"he shall bear his iniquity": this is a stock legal phrase. Reading "iniquity" as named for its punishment, and not "bear" as the figure, is an interpretive step a commentary supplies, and the Hebrew word covers guilt and punishment in its ordinary sense. In doubt.
"Whoever eats it will bear his iniquity": the same stock phrase. That the iniquity is named for its punishment is not plain from the words, so it is in doubt.
"he shall bear his iniquity": the stock phrase again. Which word carries a figure, and whether it is one, depends on interpretation.
"both shall bear their iniquity": the stock legal phrase, where the Hebrew word normally covers guilt. A cause-for-effect figure is not plain to a reader.
"They will bear their sin; they shall die childless": the same stock idiom, dropped like the other places that use it, since the metonymy reading is in doubt.
"Any man of the house of Israel" comes right after "all the Israelites" and reads as the nation's name. "House" as family line is an ordinary sense, so the figure is not plainly seen.

The BSB's "until the will of the LORD should be made clear" shows no figure. The Hebrew "al pi" ("on the mouth of") is a set compound meaning "according to", and the tags also point at "on" and "Yahweh", which do not carry any figure.

places.words_why: "I will bring a sword against you ... you will be delivered into the hand of the enemy": the sword plainly stands for war and slaughter. The figure is carried by "a sword", not by the verb and preposition beside it.

places.why: "according to the word of the LORD" is plain English with no figure. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound for "according to", and the tags on "on" and "Yahweh" do not point at a figure.
"at the LORD's command" shows no figure in the BSB. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set prepositional phrase, and the tags include "on" and "Yahweh".

'al pi YHWH ("in obedience to the word of the LORD") is mouth for command, but the H3068G tag also marks the second Yahweh in "just as the LORD had commanded him". Tags are roots and cannot be narrowed, and without them the BSB's English shows no mouth, so the place cannot be shown rightly.

'al pi Aharon ("at the direction of Aaron and his sons") is mouth for command, but the H5921A tag also marks 'alehem ("to them"), which is no part of it. The tags cannot be narrowed, and without them the English shows no mouth, so the place stays out.
"according to the command of the LORD" carries no figure in English. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound, and the tags are not limited to a figure-bearing word.
"at the LORD's command": no figure in the BSB. The Hebrew "al pi" means "according to" as a set phrase, and the tags include "on" and "Yahweh".
"numbered at the LORD's command": no figure in the BSB. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound, and the tags are wrong.

"At the LORD's command" ('al pi YHWH) is mouth for command, but the tags also mark the two 'al of "on his service ... on his burden" and the Yahweh of "as the LORD had commanded Moses". They cannot be narrowed, and the English alone shows no mouth.
"the woman shall bear her iniquity": the stock legal phrase. Reading iniquity as named for its punishment is in doubt, as in the other places that use it.

The two 'al pi YHWH ("at the LORD's command") are mouth for command, but the H5921A tag also marks 'al "over" in "over the tabernacle". The tags cannot be narrowed, and without them the English shows no mouth, so the place stays out.

The three 'al pi YHWH phrases are mouth for command, but the H3068G tag also marks the Yahweh of "the LORD's charge" (mishmeret YHWH), which has no mouth. The tags cannot be narrowed, and the English alone does not show the figure.
"according to the LORD's command through Moses": no figure in English. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound, and the tags include "on" and "Yahweh".
"at the consent of the LORD": no figure in English. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set phrase for "according to", and the tags are wrong.

"transgressing the commandment of the LORD" renders "the mouth of Yahweh", but the tags include H0853, the object marker 'et, which carries nothing. Stripping the tags leaves English that shows no mouth, so the place cannot go live as it stands.
"Aaron's staff, representing the house of Levi" uses the stock name for the tribe, and "house" for a family line is ordinary English. The figure is not plainly seen, so it stays out.
"must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary": here it means bearing responsibility for offenses, a stock phrase. A figure carried by "iniquity" is not plain.
"they must bear their iniquity": the stock phrase, and whose iniquity is meant is itself unclear. The figure is not plain.
"the entire house of Israel mourned for him" stands beside "the whole congregation" as the nation's usual name. The family sense of "house" is ordinary, so the figure is not plainly seen.

places.words_why: "If You will deliver this people into our hands": a whole people cannot be put into hands, so "hands" plainly stands for power over them, the way "the world" stands for its people. Only "our hands" carries the figure. The verb and its object do not.
"I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land": a king, his people and his land cannot go into a hand, so "hand" plainly means power. Mark only "your hand".

places.why: "Moab was terrified of the people" uses Moab, the nation's own name. It is not plain that the land is named for its people rather than the people simply named, so with that doubt it stays out.

"the command of the LORD my God" renders "the mouth of Yahweh", but the tags include H0853, the object marker 'et (word 17). Without the tags the English shows no mouth, so the place cannot be shown rightly.

places.words_why: "How lovely are your tents, O Jacob": Balaam is looking at the tribes camped below (24:2), so the ancestor's name "Jacob" plainly stands for his descendants. The "O" only marks the address and does not carry the figure.

places.why: "the command of the LORD" renders 'et pi YHWH, but the tags mark both object markers (words 11 and 22) and the Yahweh of "whatever the LORD says". They cannot be narrowed, and the English alone shows no mouth.

"A star will come forth from Jacob ... He will crush the skulls of Moab": only the picture, a star, is given, and the coming ruler ("I see him") is left implied. That is a likeness only implied, not one thing named for another. The mark is the word carrying it, "A star".

'al piv, "on his mouth", behind "At his command" is mouth for command, but the tags include H3318G, the verb "they will go out", which is no part of it. Without the tags the English shows no mouth, so the place stays out.
"then he will bear her iniquity": the stock legal phrase. Whether "iniquity" is named for its punishment is in doubt, so this is dropped like the others.
"At the LORD's command, Moses recorded": no figure in the BSB. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound, and the tags include "on" and "Yahweh".
"At the LORD's command, Aaron the priest climbed Mount Hor": no figure in English. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set phrase, and the tags are wrong.

lefi 'edim, "to the mouth of witnesses", behind "on the testimony of the witnesses" is mouth for testimony, but the H5707 tag also marks ve'ed in "a lone witness", where there is no mouth. The tags cannot be narrowed, and the English alone shows no figure.
"So at the word of the LORD, Moses commanded": no figure in the BSB. The Hebrew "al pi" is a set compound, and the tags point at "on" and "Yahweh" too.

"the mouth of Yahweh" for His command is a real figure, but it shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags light the object marker 'et (H0853) as part of it, which is wrong. With the tags removed, the BSB "the command of the LORD" shows no figure, so the place cannot go live as it stands. It could return tagged with H6310I alone, on "the command of the LORD".

places.words_why: "to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be annihilated": a whole nation put into a hand plainly means into the Amorites' power. The figure is "the hand", not "deliver us".

places.why: The BSB words are right and the Hebrew "mouth of Yahweh" plainly stands for His command. But the figure shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags light the object marker 'et (H0853), which carries nothing. Without the tags the BSB "the command of the LORD" shows no figure, so it stays out. It could return tagged with H6310I alone.

places.words_why: "I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land": a king and his land in a hand plainly means into your power. Mark "your hand" without the verb.
"that He might deliver him into your hand": a king and his land are not put in a literal hand, so "hand" plainly stands for power. The figure is in "your hand", not in the verb "deliver him into".
"I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land": "hand" plainly stands for power. Mark only "your hand".

places.why: The BSB reads "that sinful thing, the calf", which describes the calf and names nothing in its place. The Hebrew "your sin" is not shown, and the search's note rests on a commentary, so a reader of these words sees no figure.

"rebelled against the command of the LORD" renders "the mouth of Yahweh", but that shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags are wrong. H0853 lights three object markers. H3068G also lights the Yahweh in "And when the LORD sent you", and the first marked span, "And when the LORD", carries no figure. Removing the tags leaves no visible figure, so it stays out.

places.words_why: "He is your praise and He is your God": God is named by the praise given to Him, which a reader sees is not literal. The figure lies in "your praise", not in "He is", so mark fewer words.

places.why: "on the mouth of two witnesses" for testimony shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags are wrong. H5707 also lights "a witness" in "A lone witness", H8147 tags "two" while "three" is left out, and the separate mark "witness" carries no figure. Without the tags the BSB "by the testimony of" shows no figure.

places.words_why: "When the LORD your God has delivered it into your hand": a city given into a hand, so "hand" stands for power. Mark "your hand".

places.why: "on their mouth" for the priests' ruling shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags take in "it will be" (H1961), both "every" (H3605) and "dispute" (H7379). None of those carry the figure, and the span runs on into "in every dispute and". Without the tags the BSB "to give a ruling" shows no figure.

places.words_why: "the LORD your God delivers them into your hand and you take them captive": "hand" plainly stands for power over the enemies. Mark "your hand".

places.why: "you hang his body on a tree" is a literal instruction. The BSB already says "body", and nothing in these words is named for something else.
"you must not leave the body on the tree overnight" is literal: a dead body on a tree. No word stands for another thing.

The marked word "will" carries no figure. The tag on lashon is the right word, but its gloss shown is "language", not "tongue", so the reader is not plainly shown a tongue named for speech. In doubt, it stays out.

places.words_why: "there is no one who can deliver from My hand": "hand" plainly stands for God's power. Mark "My hand", not the verb.

places.why: The oath is spoken in full ("As surely as I live forever"), so the gesture does not stand in place of the oath, and metonymy is the wrong form. What plainly shows is God speaking of His own hand and a human gesture of swearing: "I lift up My hand to heaven". That is a human part said of God, as both readers proposed.

In "they are your life, and by them you will live long", the verse itself shows that the words are called "life" because they bring it: effect named for cause. The span began with a stray "you," from "idle words to you" and is now "they are your life".
places.words_why: "because they are your life, and by them you will live long": the verse itself shows the words are called "life" because they give it. The figure lies in "your life", not in "they are".

"his blood will be on his own head, and we will be innocent": the verse shows "blood" stands for the guilt of his death. Under metonymy the figure is carried by "his blood" ("his own head" is a different figure), and it carries the same sense in both of its places in the verse.
"The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands": a whole land cannot be put in literal hands, so "hands" stands for power. Mark "our hands".
"I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men": "hand" plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand".
"to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites to be destroyed": "hand" plainly stands for the Amorites' power. Mark "the hand of the Amorites", not "deliver us into".
"I have delivered into your hand the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land": "hand" plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand".
"the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand": a city given into a hand, so "hand" means power. Mark "your hand".

places.why: "He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening" is a literal account, and the verse goes on to name "the body". No word is named for another.

"the counsel of the LORD" renders "[the] mouth of Yahweh ... they did not ask", a real figure, but it shows only in the Hebrew. The tags light "and <obj.>" (H0853), which carries nothing. Without the tags the BSB shows no figure, so it stays out. It could return tagged with H6310I alone.

"delivered them from the hands of the Israelites, and they did not kill the Gibeonites": the hands plainly stand for Israel's power to kill them. The span ended on a dangling "of" and took in the verb "delivered them". It is now "the hands of the Israelites".

places.words_why: "I have delivered them into your hand. Not one of them shall stand against you": "hand" plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand".
"the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand": "hand" stands for power over the fleeing enemies. Mark "your hand".
"delivered that city and its king into the hand of Israel": "hand" plainly stands for Israel's power. The figure is in "the hand of Israel", not in "delivered that city and its king".
"the LORD delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel": "hand" plainly stands for power. Mark "the hand of Israel".

places.why: In "the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel", "hand" plainly stands for Israel's power. But the marked words "delivered them into the hand" take in the literal verb and its object and leave out "of Israel", whose hand it is. Earlier rulings set the span as the hand itself ("His hands", "My hand"), not the verb phrase, so this span fails.

The BSB says "According to the LORD's command", which shows no figure. The "mouth" (H6310) behind it is only in the Hebrew, and two of the three tags point at words that are not the figure (H0413 "to" and H3068 "Yahweh"). With the tags stripped the reader would see a plain phrase.

"in keeping with the command of the LORD" renders 'el pi Yahweh, a real figure that shows only in the Hebrew. But the separate mark "The LORD" (from "The LORD commanded Moses") carries no figure. The tag H3068G lights that Yahweh at index 11 as well as the one in the figure, and it cannot be narrowed. Without the tags the BSB shows no figure, so it stays out.

"the house of Joseph—to Ephraim and Manasseh" uses "house" in its ordinary sense of a family line, as a set name for the Joseph tribes. A reader would not take it as a figure unless a commentary said so.
"the house of Joseph shall remain in their territory in the north" is a set name for the tribes, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family, not a figure a reader would notice.
The BSB says "as the LORD had commanded", which shows no figure. "mouth" (H6310) is only in the Hebrew, and the tags also take in H5921 "on" and H3068 "Yahweh", which are not the figure.

The Hebrew 'el-pi Yahweh, "at the mouth of Yahweh", does put mouth for the command it speaks. But the tags also fall on the preposition 'el and the name Yahweh, which do not carry the figure, so they cannot stand. Without them, the BSB's "by the command of the LORD" shows no figure. It could come back tagged only H6310.

"the LORD delivered all their enemies into their hand": whole armies cannot lie in a hand, so hand plainly stands for Israel's power. The figure is carried by "their hand", not by the verb and its object.
"the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel": "house of Israel" is a set name for the nation, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family, not a figure a reader would see without being told.

'al-pi Yahweh, "on the mouth of Yahweh", does put mouth for command. But the tags also fall on the preposition 'al and the name Yahweh, which do not carry the figure, and the span starts inside "according to" and runs into "through Moses". Without the tags, the BSB's "according to the command of the LORD" shows no figure. It could come back tagged only H6310.

"you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD": the hand plainly stands for the LORD's power to punish, and since it is a hand said of God, the closer form is a human part said of God (as with Hebrews 10:31). The span left out "the LORD" and took in "delivered the Israelites"; it should be "the hand of the LORD".
"I delivered them into your hand": the Amorite nations given over to Israel, so hand plainly stands for power. The figure is "your hand", not "delivered them".
"I delivered you from his hand": hand plainly stands for Balak's power against Israel. The figure is "his hand", not "delivered you".
"I delivered them into your hand": seven nations given over to Israel, so hand plainly stands for power. The figure is "your hand".

"As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!": a building cannot serve, and "we will serve" shows house plainly stands for the household who live in it. The figure is "my house"; "me and" does not carry it.
"I have delivered the land into their hands": a land cannot lie in hands, so hands plainly stands for Judah's power. The figure is "their hands", not "delivered the land".
"The house of Joseph also attacked Bethel" uses "house of Joseph" as a set name for the tribes, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family.
"when the house of Joseph grew in strength" is the set name for the Joseph tribes, with "house" in its ordinary sense, not a figure a reader would notice.

"He delivered them into the hands of those who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies": hands plainly stands for the power of those enemies, twice over. The span took in "delivered them" and stopped before whose hands; the figure is in the two hand phrases. "sold" is a different matter and stays out.
"saved them from the hands of those who plundered them": hands plainly stands for the plunderers' power. The span took in "saved them" and ended on "of"; the figure is the whole hand phrase.
"saved them from the hands of their enemies": hands plainly stands for the enemies' power, as "those who oppressed them" goes on to say. The span took in "saved them" and ended on "of".
"by delivering them into the hand of Joshua": whole nations given over, so hand plainly stands for Joshua's power. The figure is "the hand of Joshua", not "delivering them".

"He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim ... and the Israelites served him eight years": hand plainly stands for the king's power over them. The span took in "sold them", a separate matter, and left out whose hand.
"the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand": an army given over, so hand plainly stands for power. The figure is "your hand", not the whole clause.

"the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan", who then "harshly oppressed the Israelites for twenty years" (4:3): hand plainly stands for Jabin's power. The span took in "sold them" and left out whose hand.
"I will deliver him into your hand": Sisera with his chariots and troops given over to Barak, so hand plainly stands for power. The figure is "your hand".
"the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand": Sisera and his army given over, so hand plainly stands for Barak's power. The figure is "your hand", not "delivered Sisera".

"He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years": hand plainly stands for Midian's power, and the next verse, "the hand of Midian prevailed against Israel", confirms it. The span took in "delivered them" and left out "of Midian".

"I delivered you out of the hands of Egypt and all your oppressors": a nation's hands are its power, so the figure is plain. The span took in "delivered you" and ended on "of"; the figure is "the hands of Egypt".
"the LORD has forsaken us and delivered us into the hand of Midian": hand plainly stands for Midian's power. The figure is "the hand of Midian", not "delivered us".

A whole people is given into the plunderers' power, so this is plainly hand for power. The span is cut to the figure.
places.words_why: "delivered them into the hands of plunderers" plainly uses "hands" for the plunderers' power over Israel. "into" does not carry the figure.

places.why: "torn Israel away from the house of David" uses the standing name for David's royal line. A reader takes "house" in its ordinary sense of dynasty and would not see a figure without being told.
"the hands of all your enemies" is plainly the enemies' power. The span is cut to drop "deliver you" and the dangling "of".
"my hand" is plainly the Assyrian king's power and army. The span is cut to the figure.
places.words_why: "he cannot deliver you from my hand": the people of Jerusalem are not in the king's real hand, so "my hand" plainly stands for his power. "from" is not the figure.
"this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria": a city is not put in a real hand, so "hand" plainly stands for his power. The mark should be the hand phrase, not "given into".

places.why: "the hand of the king of Assyria" is plainly his power. The span is cut to drop "delivered his land".
"my hand" is plainly the king's power. The span is cut to drop "delivered Samaria", which is a different matter (a city for its people).
places.words_why: "Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?": a city is not held in a real hand, so "my hand" plainly stands for power. "from" is not part of it.

places.why: "my hand" is plainly the king's power, and the verse uses it in both questions. The span is cut to drop "delivered his land". Both times "from my hand" appears it carries the figure.
places.words_why: "has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" plainly puts "my hand" for the king's power, both times. "from" is not the figure.
"Jerusalem will not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria" plainly uses "hand" for his power over the city. The mark should be the hand phrase, not "delivered into".

places.why: "his hand" is plainly Sennacherib's power. The span is cut to drop "save us".
places.words_why: "please save us from his hand": the people are not in Sennacherib's real hand, so "his hand" plainly stands for his power. "from" is not the figure.

places.why: "the surviving remnant of the house of Judah" uses the set name for the nation, as "house of Israel" is, and the verse's own figure is the plant image "take root below and bear fruit above". A reader takes "house of Judah" as a name, not as a figure.
"the hand of the king of Assyria" is plainly his power. The span is cut to drop "deliver you and this city".

"the plumb line used against the house of Ahab" sets the house inside a builder's image of measuring lines and plumb lines, so a reader cannot plainly see "house" as only named for a family here. When in doubt, it does not go live.
"the hands of their enemies" is plainly the enemies' power, and the next clause says they become plunder. The span is cut to the figure.
places.words_why: "deliver them into the hands of their enemies" plainly uses "hands" for the enemies' power over the people. "into" is not part of the figure.

places.why: In English, "abomination" already means a detestable thing, so "Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians" reads as a plain judgment, not as one thing named for another. Readers would need a commentary to see a metonymy here. When in doubt, drop.

In the Hebrew, 'al pi Par'oh ("on the mouth of Pharaoh") is mouth for command, but the BSB "Pharaoh's demand" shows no figure, so the place depends on its tags. Those tags are wrong: H6547T also marks "to Pharaoh" at words 4 and 26, and it marks the name rather than the figure word. The first span, "to Pharaoh Neco", carries no figure either. Stripping the tags would leave only plain English, so the place cannot go live as built.

In the Hebrew, 'al pi YHWH ("on the mouth of Yahweh") is mouth for command, but the BSB "at the LORD's command" shows no figure, so the place depends on its tags. Those tags are wrong: H5921A also marks me'al ("from", word 7), which the second span "from" picks up, and H3068G marks the name, not the figure word. Stripping the tags would leave only plain English, so it cannot go live as built.

The verse itself spells out that "all Jerusalem" means its people: "all the commanders and mighty men...ten thousand captives". The city is named for those in it. The span is cut to drop "carried into exile".

places.words_why: "the Hagrites and all their allies were delivered into their hands": whole peoples are not put in real hands, so "their hands" plainly stands for power. "delivered into" is not the figure.

places.why: The BSB reads "in accordance with the word of the LORD", which shows no figure; the Hebrew kefi, "according to the mouth of", is the set idiom for "according to", and the tag on "Yahweh" is a name, not the figure. A reader would need to be told that a figure lies under it.

The Hebrew reads only "the leader of Aaron" (le'aharon), so "house" was added by the translator. The marked figure is not in the Bible's own words. "house of Aaron" for the priestly family is also a plain idiom, not a figure a reader would notice.
"remained loyal to the house of Saul" names Saul's family and line by its usual name. "House" for a family is an ordinary sense of the word, so the figure is not plain enough to go live.
The Philistines given "into my hand" plainly means into David's power in battle, and the LORD's answer "into your hand" says it again. The span is cut to drop "deliver them".
places.words_why: "Will You deliver them into my hand?" and "I will deliver them into your hand" plainly put "hand" for David's power over the Philistine army. Both hand phrases carry the figure; "into" does not.

places.why: In "call upon His name" the name may simply be the name that is called out. It is not plain that "name" stands for God Himself, so the doubt counts against it.
The earth is told to sing and to proclaim His salvation, so "all the earth" plainly means its people, the earth for its people. The span is cut to the figure.

"tremble before Him, all the earth" can be read as the land itself quaking before God (the next line speaks of the physical world, "The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved", and 16:31 has "the earth rejoice"). It is not plain that the earth is put for its people.
"Your holy name" stands for God Himself, whom the same prayer calls on as "O God of our salvation". This is a name for the person. The span is cut to drop "give thanks to".

places.words_why: "I will establish his throne forever" comes right after "I will establish his kingdom", so the throne plainly stands for his reign. Mark only the noun, not the verb.
In "his throne will be established forever", after "My house and My kingdom", the seat plainly stands for his reign. Mark only "his throne".

places.why: "the sword of the LORD—days of plague" could be metonymy (the weapon for the death it brings) or metaphor (the plague called a sword). The angel also holds a real drawn sword in 21:16, so even the figure is unsure. The span takes in the explaining words "days of plague" too. When in doubt, drop.

places.words_why: In "fall into the hand of the LORD ... fall into the hands of men" the hand plainly stands for power. Mark the two hand phrases, not "fall into".
In "establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever" the throne plainly stands for royal rule. Mark the noun, not the verb.

places.why: A people cannot be put into a hand, so "into my hand" plainly means into David's power: the hand is named for the power it goes with. The marked words also took in the object "the inhabitants of the land", which plays no part in the figure. Only "into my hand" carries it.
places.words_why: In "He has given the inhabitants of the land into my hand" a whole people is given into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for power. Mark "my hand".

places.why: "the house of Judah" is a set name for the tribe, and "house" is used in its ordinary sense of a family line. A reader takes it as a name, not as a figure.

places.words_why: "we give You thanks, and we praise Your glorious name" sets "You" beside "Your glorious name", so the name plainly stands for God. Mark the name, not the verb.

places.why: "the house of David" is the set name of David's dynasty, with "house" in its ordinary sense of a family line. A reader would not see a figure there without being told.
"mobilized the house of Judah and Benjamin" uses "house of Judah" as the set name of the tribe, in the ordinary sense of family. It is not plainly a figure.

places.words_why: In "God delivered them into their hands" a fleeing army is put into hands, so the hands plainly stand for power. Mark "their hands" only.
In "a vast army with many chariots and horsemen ... He delivered them into your hand" the hand plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand" only.
In "God will deliver it into the hand of the king" a city, Ramoth-gilead, is given into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for the king's power. Mark only the hand, not "deliver it".
"the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king" puts a city into a hand, so the hand plainly means power. Mark the hand only.
In "they will be given into your hand" an enemy army is given into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand".

places.why: "the ruler of the house of Judah" uses the set name of the tribe, with "house" in its ordinary sense. A reader would not see a figure without being told.

Listed as a disaster beside plague and famine, "sword" plainly stands for war, the weapon named for what it brings. "Judgment", "plague" and "famine" are meant literally, so the marked words narrow to "sword" alone.
"just as the house of Ahab had done" uses the set name of Ahab's dynasty, with "house" in its ordinary sense of a family line. It is not plainly a figure.
"the house of David" is the set name of David's dynasty, and the verse goes on "David and his descendants". "House" is used in its ordinary sense, so this is not plainly a figure.
"just as the house of Ahab prostituted itself" names Ahab's dynasty by its set name, with "house" in its ordinary sense. When in doubt, drop.
"walked in the ways of the house of Ahab" uses the set name of Ahab's family line. "House" is in its ordinary sense, so this is not plainly a figure.
"as the house of Ahab had done" uses the set name of Ahab's dynasty, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family. When in doubt, drop.
"to destroy the house of Ahab" names the dynasty by its set name, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family. It is not plainly a figure.
"executing judgment on the house of Ahab" uses the set name of Ahab's family line, with "house" in its ordinary sense. When in doubt, drop.
"no one was left from the house of Ahaziah" uses "house" in its ordinary sense of family. A reader would not see a figure there without being told.
"all the royal heirs of the house of Judah" uses the set name of the royal line, with "house" in its ordinary sense of family. It is not plainly a figure.

places.words_why: In "the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army" a whole army is put into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for power. Mark "their hand".
In "which could not deliver them from your hand" the hand plainly stands for Amaziah's power over the people. Mark "your hand" only.
In "deliver them into the hand of Jehoash" a whole army is given into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for power. Mark the hand, not the verb.

"delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Aram ... into the hand of the king of Israel": the hand plainly stands for power, and the next words are "who attacked him". Mark the two hand phrases, not the verb or "Ahaz".
In "the LORD ... has delivered them into your hand" captives of war are given into a hand, so the hand plainly stands for power. Mark "your hand".

places.why: "they ate the Passover" reads as the ordinary words for eating the Passover meal. A reader would not see the feast's name put for the lamb without being told.

places.words_why: In "deliver us from the hand of the king of Assyria" the hand plainly stands for the king's power. The verb "deliver us from" is not part of the figure.
In "deliver their land from my hand", "my hand" plainly means the Assyrian king's power. "their land" could be the territory itself, so only "my hand" is kept.
In "deliver his people from my hand" and "deliver you from my hand", the hand plainly stands for the king's power. The verb and "his people" do not carry the figure.
In "from my hand or from the hand of my fathers", the hand plainly stands for the power of the Assyrian kings. The marked words ran on to "deliver his people" and stopped at a dangling "of".
In "did not deliver their people from my hand", "my hand" plainly means the king's power. The verb and "their people" are not the figure.

places.why: The plain picture in "My wrath will be poured out ... and will not be quenched" is wrath pictured as a liquid poured out and a fire that is not quenched. That is an implied likeness made through the verbs, not a clean metaphor and not one thing named for another. Reading "wrath" as standing for punishment needs a commentary, and no live form fits the marked words plainly, so it is dropped.

places.words_why: In "God gave them all into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar", the hand plainly stands for his power. The marked words left out whose hand it was and included "gave them all".
In "Those who escaped the sword", the sword plainly stands for the killing done with it. "escaped" is the verb, not the figure.

places.why: The BSB reads "through Jeremiah". The Hebrew befi, "by [the] mouth of Jeremiah", reads naturally as literal, because the prophet did speak the word, so mouth standing for speech is not plain here (unlike "according to the mouth of Pharaoh"). The whole verse is marked, and the tag on the name Jeremiah (H3414L) does not carry any figure. Dropped when in doubt.

This is the same phrase as 36:21. "Spoken through Jeremiah" renders befi, "by [the] mouth of", which reads literally, since Jeremiah spoke it with his mouth, so it does not plainly show one thing named for another. The tag on the name Jeremiah (H3414L) does not point at any figure. Dropped when in doubt.

places.words_why: In "He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar", the hand plainly stands for his power. The verb is not part of the figure, and the owner of the hand was missing.

In "delivered into the hands of the kings of the earth", the hands plainly stand for the kings' power. The marked words held the verb "delivered into" and left out whose hands they were, so they are cut to the hands and their owners.

places.why: In the BSB, "the joy of the LORD is your strength" reads as a plain statement that this joy makes them strong. Seeing "strength" as named for its cause needs a commentary. The Hebrew word is ma'oz, "refuge", which would make it a picture of a stronghold rather than a metonymy, and the BSB's "strength" does not show that. Neither form is plain at the marked words, so it is dropped.

"You delivered into their hands the kings and peoples of the land": nobody holds kings and peoples in literal hands, so "hands" plainly stands for their power. The word that carries it is "their hands", not the verb.

"delivered them into the hands of enemies who oppressed them ... saved them from the hands of their enemies": a whole nation in hands plainly means in the enemies' power. The figure is in "the hands", and both phrases carry it.
The BSB reads "the language of the other peoples" and the gloss shown reads "language of", so no reader sees a tongue standing for speech. The marked words "or of" carry nothing.
"to each people in their own language": the BSB and the gloss shown both read "language", so no word plainly stands for another. The second tagged word has no BSB words at all.
"the language of every people": the word reads plainly as "language" in the BSB and the gloss, so no figure shows. The marked span "language of every" also breaks the phrase.
"the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion": a city cannot be confused, so it plainly stands for its people. The words that carry it are "the city of Susa".
"to every people in their own language ... their own script and language": the BSB and the gloss shown both read "language", so no figure is plain. The marked "and to" carries nothing.

"deliver me from the hand of the enemy; redeem me from the grasp of the ruthless": the parallel "grasp" and the word "redeem" show that "hand" plainly means the enemy's power. The words that carry it are "the hand of the enemy".
"The earth is given into the hand of the wicked": nobody holds the earth in a literal hand, so "hand" plainly stands for their power. The words that carry it are "the hand of the wicked".

"all who take refuge in You ... those who love Your name may rejoice in You": the same line goes from "Your name" to "You", which plainly shows the name standing for God Himself. The words that carry it are "Your name".
"I will thank the LORD ... and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High": the paired lines show the name standing for the LORD. The words that carry it are the whole phrase, without the verb.
"rejoice in You; I will sing praise to Your name": the parallel "in You" plainly shows that "Your name" is God Himself. The words that carry it are "Your name".
"He has established His throne for judgment" can be read of God's actual seat of judgment (compare 9:4). The throne standing for His rule is possible but not plain, so the place stays out.

The BSB words "a scorching wind will be their portion" show no figure, since the BSB leaves "cup" out. In the Hebrew "portion of their cup" it is not plain whether the cup names its contents or pictures their fate as a drink, and "will be" carries nothing.

"they speak with flattering lips and a double heart": lips cannot flatter, so "lips" plainly stands for their speech. The tags cover the Hebrew "a lip of flatteries", the same phrase as the marked words. The second mark "lips" only repeated part of the first, so it is removed.

"May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue": with "cut off", the lips may stand for the flatterers themselves (a part for the whole) or for their speech. Which form it is is not plain, so the place stays out.

"With our tongues we will prevail. We own our lips, who can be our master?": coming after 12:2 and 12:3, tongues and lips plainly stand for what they say. The words that carry it are "our tongues" and "our lips", not "we will prevail".
"When the LORD restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice": the forefather's name plainly stands for the people descended from him. The word that carries it is "Jacob".
"The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup" plainly says the LORD is a portion and a cup, which He is like. That is a metaphor. Reading the cup as its contents takes a further step that is not plain.
"I will praise You, O LORD ... I will sing praises to Your name": the parallel plainly shows that "Your name" is the LORD Himself. The words that carry it are "Your name".

"Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God": set against chariots and horses, trusting in the name plainly means trusting the LORD Himself. The words that carry it are the whole phrase, without "trust in".

"You lay me in the dust of death" is figurative, but it is not plain whether dust names the grave (metonymy) or the line pictures him brought near death. It can also be read of burial in the ground, so the place stays out.
"Deliver my soul from the sword" reads naturally as a plea to be saved from a real sword, so the sword standing for something else is not plain. The mark also takes the whole line.
"for the sake of His name": here "name" reads as God's honor or reputation, a sense the English word already has. Nothing in the verse shows it standing for something else.

"For the sake of Your name, O LORD, forgive my iniquity": "name" reads as God's honor or reputation, an ordinary sense of the word, and no parallel line shows it standing for the person. The figure is not plain.

"The LORD is my strength and my shield": the LORD is not the quality strength but the One who gives it, so He is plainly named for what He gives. The figure is carried by "my strength"; the old span dropped "The" and took in the subject.
"The LORD is the strength of His people" reads as ordinary speech for the giver of strength, or as a metaphor. A careful reader would not see a metonymy here without being told.
"Sing to the LORD ... and praise His holy name": the paired lines show that His name stands for the LORD Himself. The figure is carried by "His holy name", not the verb "praise".

"in my descent to the Pit? Will the dust praise You?": dust cannot praise, and after the Pit it plainly stands for the dead man gone to the grave. The figure is carried by "the dust". The rest of the span is the question, which is a different figure.

"lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name": here "name" reads as God's honor or reputation, which the English word already means. Nothing in the verse shows it standing for something else, so the figure is not plain.

"Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the people of the world revere Him": the second line shows that the earth stands for its people. The figure is carried by "all the earth"; "fear" is not part of it.
"our hearts rejoice in Him, since we trust in His holy name": the parallel "in Him" shows that the name stands for God Himself. The figure is carried by "His holy name", not "trust in".
"Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together": "His name" restates "the LORD", so the name plainly stands for the LORD Himself. The figure is carried by "His name", without the verb.

"The mouth of the righteous man utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice": the mouth and tongue do just what they literally do, so it is not plain that anything is named for something else. The span also cuts off "man".

"Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom": next to the throne that endures, the scepter, the sign a king rules with, plainly stands for His rule. The Hebrew says the same thing as "a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom". The figure is carried by "scepter of Your kingdom".

"You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue": a tongue cannot love, so the man is spoken to by one part of himself. That is a part for the whole, so it belongs under synecdoche rather than metonymy. "deceitful tongue" is the right phrase.

"When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice": coming right after "His captive people", the forefather's name plainly stands for the people descended from him. The figure is carried by "Jacob", not "let ... rejoice".
"Freely I will sacrifice to You; I will praise Your name, O LORD": the parallel "to You" shows that the name stands for the LORD. The figure is carried by "Your name", without "praise".

"reserved for those who fear Your name": nothing in the verse sets the name beside God Himself, and a reader takes "Your name" as the usual phrase, the name of God. The figure is not plain, so it is dropped.
"Then I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day": no parallel line puts the name for God Himself. "Praise to Your name" reads as the usual phrase, so in doubt it is dropped.
In "with joyful lips my mouth will praise You" the lips and mouth really are what praise comes from. Nothing is plainly named in place of something else.
"The mouths of liars will be shut" speaks of real mouths closed, meaning the liars are silenced. A metonymy is not plain here.
"Sing to God! Sing praises to His name" sets His name beside God Himself, so the name stands for the person. The carrier is "His name" (its first use, line 2).
places.words_why: "Sing to God! Sing praises to His name" puts the name plainly in the place of God. But "His name" comes twice, and in "His name is the LORD" it is the literal name, so only the first one is marked.

places.why: The plain picture in "Pour out Your wrath" is wrath poured like a liquid, which is not this form. Reading wrath as put for its punishment needs a commentary, and no live form fits the pouring cleanly.

"The descendants of His servants will inherit it, and those who love His name will settle in it": the parallel sets people beside people, not the name beside God. "His name" can be read in its ordinary sense, so in doubt it is dropped.
"From the hand of the wicked", beside "from the grasp of the unjust", plainly puts the hand for their power. The marked words left out "the wicked" and took in the plea.

"God is the strength of my heart" reads as ordinary speech for the giver of strength, or as a metaphor, and the marked "God is the strength" is a clause, not a figure. A careful reader would not see a metonymy here without being told.
"may the poor and needy praise Your name": nothing in the verse sets the name for God Himself, and "praise Your name" reads as the usual phrase. In doubt, it is dropped.
"Lied to Him with their tongues" names the tongue as what they lied with, which is literal. Nothing is plainly named in place of something else.

In "for the glory of Your name ... for the sake of Your name", "name" reads most naturally in its ordinary sense of renown or reputation. Seeing it as put for God Himself takes a commentary, so it is dropped.

"revive us, and we will call on Your name": calling on the name reads as the ordinary act of calling on His name in prayer. "Not turn away from You" is a different act, not a restatement, so the figure is not plain.

The BSB reads "I heard an unfamiliar language", which has no figure in it. The tagged word H8193K is shown as "a language", the word's own "language" sense (the "lip" sense is H8193G), so a reader would see "lip for language" only if a lexicon told them.
"Save them from the hand of the wicked" plainly puts the hand for the wicked's power. The marked words cut off "the wicked" and took in the verb.
"Bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name" sets the name beside the Lord Himself, so it stands for the person. The carrier is "Your name".
"Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name": the line beside it is "that I may walk in Your truth", and no line in the verse sets the name for God Himself. In doubt, it is dropped.
"I will praise You ... I will glorify Your name": the parallel line shows that the name stands for God Himself. The carrier is "Your name".
"To praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name": the parallel shows that the name stands for the LORD Himself. The carrier is "Your name".
"Sing to the LORD, all the earth" calls the earth's people to sing; 96:3 names the nations. The earth is put for its people, and only "all the earth" carries it.
"Sing to the LORD, bless His name": the name, set beside the LORD, stands for the person. The carrier is "His name".
"Worship the LORD ... tremble before Him, all the earth" calls the earth's people to worship. The earth is put for its people; the carrier is "all the earth".
"He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness": the parallel with "the peoples" plainly shows the world put for its people. The carrier is "the world".
"He delivers them from the hand of the wicked" plainly puts the hand for the wicked's power. The marked words cut off "the wicked" and took in the verb.
"Rejoice in the LORD ... and praise His holy name": the name, set beside the LORD, stands for the person. The carrier is "His holy name".
"the house of Israel" is a set name for the people of Israel. A reader takes it as a name, not as a figure they can see in the words.
"Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth", followed by lyre and harp in 98:5, calls the earth's people to praise. Only "all the earth" carries the figure, not the whole line.
"He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity": the parallel with "the peoples" shows the world put for its people. The carrier is "the world".
"Those who called on His name. They called to the LORD": the next line plainly shows the name standing for the LORD Himself. The carrier is "His name".

"Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth", followed by "Serve the LORD with gladness" (100:2), plainly calls the earth's people, so the earth stands for its people. The marked span ran across two BSB lines. Only "all the earth" carries the figure.
In "give thanks to Him and bless His name", the name set beside "Him" plainly stands for God Himself. The figure is carried by "His name", not by the verb "bless".

"The nations will fear the name of the LORD" stands beside "will fear Your glory", so the name plainly stands for the LORD Himself. The marked span "fear the name" took in the verb and cut off "of the LORD".
"He is mindful that we are dust" reads as a plain statement or a metaphor of what man is made of; a reader would not see one thing named for another here without a commentary.
"The LORD has established His throne in heaven" can be read as God's actual throne in heaven. A reader does not need to take "throne" as standing for His rule, so the place is doubtful.
"Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name": the name set beside the LORD plainly stands for the person. The figure is carried by "His name", not by "call upon".

In "He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known", "name" means renown, which is an ordinary English sense of the word ("a good name"). A reader would not see one thing named for another without being told.

A hand does not hate, so "the hand that hated them" (set beside "the hand of the enemy") plainly puts the hand for the enemy's power. The marked span "saved them from the hand" took in the verb and cut off "that hated them".

The BSB says "and swore" outright, so the raised hand is not named in place of the oath, and the verse is not a metonymy. What a reader plainly sees is a human hand and a human gesture said of God, so it belongs under human parts said of God, at "He raised His hand".
places.words_why: "So He raised His hand and swore" plainly gives God the human gesture of an oath. The figure is in "raised His hand", not the pronoun before it.

places.why: "He delivered them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them": the words after show that the hand plainly means the nations' power and rule. The marked span took in the verb and cut off "of the nations".

"Save us, O LORD our God ... that we may give thanks to Your holy name": the thanks go to God himself, so the name plainly stands for Him. The figure is carried by "Your holy name", not by "give thanks to".

The BSB reads "waiting to catch Him in something He might say." The words are plain, with nothing named for anything else. The metonymy ("mouth" put for words) is only in the Greek, which this place does not show.

In "whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me", the whole clause is a picture of a condemned man walking to his death. That is a likeness implied (hypocatastasis), not plainly "his cross" named for something else, and the verse does not show what the cross stands for, so the form is in doubt.
places.words_why: In "whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me", the cross plainly stands for the suffering it brings. Mark "his cross", without the verb.
"I have sinned against heaven and against you": one cannot sin against a place, so heaven plainly stands for God. Only "heaven" carries the figure, not "sinned against".

places.why: "The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John" uses the usual names of parts of Scripture, or of the prophets themselves. Nothing plainly shows one thing named for another.
"listen to Moses and the prophets" is a set name for the Scriptures. It is the kind of set name the rules say to leave out, and a reader takes it as the ordinary name, not a figure.
"I will judge you by your own words" uses "words" in its ordinary sense. The figure ("out of your mouth") sits behind the translation, and a BSB reader would not see it.
In "was it from heaven, or from men?" heaven, set against men, plainly stands for God. Only "from heaven" carries the figure; "or from men" is literal.
places.words_why: "was it from heaven, or from men?": heaven is plainly put for God against men, but "from" is only the preposition; mark "heaven".

places.why: "I will give you speech and wisdom": the BSB has already put "speech" for the Greek "mouth", so the English word stands in its plain sense. No figure shows in these words.
"Where I may eat the Passover" uses the ordinary name for the Passover meal. A reader would not see one thing named for another here.
"And they prepared the Passover" is the ordinary way to name the Passover meal. No figure is plainly seen in the words.

"Take this and divide it among yourselves" only implies the cup for its wine through pronouns, and sharing a cup reads as ordinary speech. The marked words never name the cup, so the figure is not plain at these words.

places.words_why: In "delivered into the hands of sinful men", hands plainly stand for power. Mark the noun phrase, not "delivered into".

places.why: "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets" is a set name for the parts of Scripture. A reader takes it as the ordinary name, not as a figure he would notice.
